title: The Lucas / Kummer Digit Structure of Surviving Hasse Derivatives of Xᵐ
description: The parent entry (factor-remainder-hasse-derivative-fq-oq-01) proves the overcounting dichotomy: over a field of characteristic p the ordinary iterated-derivative multiplicity test is exact when the true root multiplicity m satisfies m < p and becomes blind once m ≥ p. Its first open question asks, in the unbounded regime m ≥ p, to stratify by the base-p digits of m — which Hasse derivatives remain nonvanishing, and how does the blindness interact with the Lucas/Kummer structure of the binomial coefficients defining hasseDeriv? This entry answers it completely for the pure power Xᵐ. The k-th Hasse derivative is the single monomial hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) = C(m,k) · X^(m-k) (hasseDeriv_X_pow), so over a characteristic-p field it is nonzero exactly when C(m,k) survives reduction mod p (hasseDeriv_X_pow_ne_zero_iff). Feeding this into Lucas's theorem resolves the question: hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) ≠ 0 iff every base-p digit of k is ≤ the corresponding digit of m (Kummer: no carries). The surviving orders are the digit-dominated k, which for m ≥ p spread all the way to k = m — while the ordinary test can only read orders k < p. The digit count ∏(dᵢ + 1) is realized concretely over 𝔽₂: X³ (11₂) keeps all four orders k ≤ 3, X⁴ (100₂) keeps only k ∈ {0,4}. 9 theorems, 0 axioms, 0 sorries.

meta.author: Lean Genius

mathlibDependencies.description: hasseDeriv k (monomial n r) = monomial (n - k) (C(n,k) · r) — with X^m = monomial m 1 this gives the closed form hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) = C(m,k) · X^(m-k), the monomial whose coefficient the entry studies mod p.

Lucas's theorem in product form: for n, k < p^a, C(n,k) ≡ ∏_{i<a} C(nᵢ, kᵢ) (mod p) where nᵢ, kᵢ are the base-p digits. The engine that turns divisibility of a single binomial into a per-digit statement.
(n : F) = 0 ↔ p ∣ n over a ring of characteristic p — the bridge translating vanishing of the coefficient C(m,k) in F into divisibility p ∣ C(m,k) in ℕ.
p ∣ n! ↔ p ≤ n for p prime — used in the single-digit engine to show p ∤ a! when a < p, hence p ∤ C(a,b) for b ≤ a < p.

originalContributions: hasseDeriv_X_pow: the closed form hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) = C(m,k) · X^(m-k) over any commutative ring, reducing a differential-operator question to a single binomial coefficient.

hasseDeriv_X_pow_ne_zero_iff / hasseDeriv_X_pow_eq_zero_iff: over a characteristic-p field, (non)vanishing of hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) ↔ ¬ p ∣ C(m,k) (resp. p ∣ C(m,k)) via CharP.cast_eq_zero_iff and monomial_eq_zero_iff.
not_dvd_choose_of_le_of_lt_prime / not_dvd_choose_digit_iff: the single-digit engine — for a base-p digit a < p, ¬ p ∣ C(a,b) ↔ b ≤ a, proved from C(a,b)·b!·(a-b)! = a! and p ∤ a!.

hasseDeriv_X_pow_ne_zero_iff_digits: the capstone. Over a field of characteristic p with m, k < p^a, hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) ≠ 0 ↔ ∀ i < a, digitᵢ(k) ≤ digitᵢ(m). Built by combining hasseDeriv_X_pow_ne_zero_iff with Lucas's product congruence and Prime.dvd_finset_prod_iff, reducing to the single-digit engine on each factor.

nonzero_orders_X3_F2, nonzero_orders_X4_F2, hasseDeriv_X4_F2_profile: the Glaisher/Fine digit count ∏(dᵢ + 1) realized over 𝔽₂ — X³ (11₂) keeps all four orders k ≤ 3, X⁴ (100₂) keeps exactly k ∈ {0,4} and vanishes at k = 1,2,3, an explicit surviving-order profile in the m ≥ p regime.

relatedProblems.relationship: Parent: proves the overcounting dichotomy (exact for m < p, unbounded overcount for m ≥ p) and asks, as its first open question, to stratify the m ≥ p regime by the base-p digits of m via the Lucas/Kummer structure of the binomials defining hasseDeriv. This entry answers it for the pure power Xᵐ with a sharp digit-domination criterion.

Grandparent: establishes the exact failure threshold (k! : F) = 0 ↔ p ≤ k of the ordinary-derivative multiplicity test and the X^{p^e} counterexample. This entry replaces the coarse threshold with the exact per-order survival set of the Hasse derivatives themselves.

overview.historicalContext: Over a field of characteristic zero the k-th ordinary derivative of Xᵐ is m(m−1)···(m−k+1)·X^(m−k), nonzero for all k ≤ m, so the derivatives faithfully read root multiplicity. In characteristic p the picture fractures. The grandparent entry pins the ordinary test's failure to the factorial threshold (k! : F) = 0 ↔ p ≤ k, and the parent turns this into an all-or-nothing dichotomy on the true multiplicity m. But the ordinary derivatives are the WRONG object in characteristic p — the Hasse (divided-power) derivatives are. Their coefficients are binomial coefficients C(m,k), whose vanishing mod p is the classical domain of Lucas (1878) and Kummer (1852): C(m,k) ≢ 0 (mod p) iff the base-p addition of k and m−k has no carries, equivalently every base-p digit of k is dominated by the corresponding digit of m.
overview.problemStatement: Over a field of characteristic p, for which orders k is the Hasse derivative hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) nonzero? In the unbounded regime m ≥ p — where the ordinary test is completely blind — describe the surviving-order set in terms of the base-p digit expansion of m.
overview.proofStrategy: Reduce the differential-operator question to arithmetic in three steps. (1) hasseDeriv_X_pow: X^m = monomial m 1 and hasseDeriv_monomial give the closed form hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) = C(m,k) · X^(m-k), a single monomial. (2) hasseDeriv_X_pow_ne_zero_iff: monomial_eq_zero_iff plus CharP.cast_eq_zero_iff turn nonvanishing of that monomial over F into ¬ p ∣ C(m,k). (3) hasseDeriv_X_pow_ne_zero_iff_digits: Lucas's product congruence (Nat.Choose.choose_modEq_prod_range_choose_nat) rewrites p ∣ C(m,k) as p dividing a product of per-digit binomials; Prime.dvd_finset_prod_iff distributes the prime over the product, and the single-digit engine not_dvd_choose_digit_iff (¬ p ∣ C(a,b) ↔ b ≤ a for a < p, from C(a,b)·b!·(a−b)! = a! and p ∤ a!) discharges each factor. The 𝔽₂ realizations bound k above by the degree with hasseDeriv_eq_zero_of_lt_natDegree and finish the finite sweep by kernel decide.
keyInsights: The Hasse derivative of a pure power is a single monomial C(m,k)·X^(m-k); the entire arithmetic content lives in the scalar C(m,k), so vanishing over 𝔽_p is exactly divisibility p ∣ C(m,k).

Lucas's theorem converts that one divisibility into a per-base-p-digit condition: p ∤ C(m,k) iff every digit of k is ≤ the corresponding digit of m — the surviving orders form the digit-domination sublattice of [0,m].

The ordinary test's blindness is orthogonal to Hasse survival. The ordinary derivatives only ever see orders k < p (each scaled by the unit k!); the genuinely surviving Hasse orders are digit-dominated k that, for m ≥ p, stretch all the way out to k = m.

The number of surviving orders is the Glaisher/Fine product ∏(dᵢ + 1) over the base-p digits dᵢ of m — realized over 𝔽₂ where it counts nonzero binomials C(m,k): X³ = 11₂ keeps all 2·2 = 4 orders, X⁴ = 100₂ keeps only 1·1·2 = 2 orders.
This exhibits the exact structure the parent's dichotomy hides: 'blind for m ≥ p' is coarse; the fine truth is a digit-carved survival pattern, sparse or full according to the base-p expansion of m.

sections.title: Overview: Lucas/Kummer digit structure of vanishing Hasse derivatives of Xᵐ
sections.summary: The imports (Polynomial.HasseDeriv, Nat.Choose.Lucas, Nat.Prime.Factorial, ZMod, Tactic), the module docstring, and the namespace/variable setup. In the unbounded regime m ≥ p — where the parent's ordinary iterated-derivative test goes blind — this file stratifies which Hasse derivatives of the pure power Xᵐ survive in characteristic p by the base-p digits of m.
sections.mathContext: For Xᵐ the k-th Hasse derivative is the single monomial hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) = C(m,k)·X^{m-k} (hasseDeriv_X_pow), so over a characteristic-p field it is nonzero exactly when ¬ p ∣ C(m,k) (hasseDeriv_X_pow_ne_zero_iff). Feeding this into Lucas's theorem gives the digit-domination (Kummer no-carry) criterion: it survives iff every base-p digit of k is ≤ the corresponding digit of m (hasseDeriv_X_pow_ne_zero_iff_digits). The number of surviving orders is ∏(dᵢ+1) over the base-p digits of m, realized over 𝔽₂ (nonzero_orders_X3_F2: X³ keeps all four orders; nonzero_orders_X4_F2: X⁴ keeps only k∈{0,4}). All results are 0-axiom, 0-sorry over any characteristic-p field.

sections.title: Closed Form and the Vanishing Criterion
sections.summary: hasseDeriv_X_pow: hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) = C(m,k) · X^(m-k) over any commutative ring, via X_pow_eq_monomial and hasseDeriv_monomial. hasseDeriv_X_pow_ne_zero_iff and hasseDeriv_X_pow_eq_zero_iff: over a characteristic-p field, (non)vanishing of that monomial is exactly ¬ p ∣ C(m,k) (resp. p ∣ C(m,k)), via monomial_eq_zero_iff and CharP.cast_eq_zero_iff.
sections.mathContext: Turns the differential operator hasseDeriv k on Xᵐ into a single binomial coefficient C(m,k), whose vanishing over 𝔽_p is the divisibility p ∣ C(m,k).

sections.title: The Single-Digit Lucas Engine
sections.summary: not_dvd_choose_of_le_of_lt_prime: for b ≤ a < p, p ∤ C(a,b), proved from C(a,b)·b!·(a-b)! = a! and Nat.Prime.dvd_factorial (p ∤ a! since a < p). not_dvd_choose_digit_iff: for a < p, ¬ p ∣ C(a,b) ↔ b ≤ a — the atomic per-digit statement that Lucas multiplies across digit positions.
sections.mathContext: A single base-p digit a < p never introduces a factor of p into C(a,b) unless b overshoots a; this is the multiplicand of Lucas's product.

sections.title: The Capstone: Lucas Digit-Domination
sections.summary: hasseDeriv_X_pow_ne_zero_iff_digits: over a field of characteristic p, with m, k < p^a, hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) ≠ 0 ↔ ∀ i < a, ⌊k/pⁱ⌋ mod p ≤ ⌊m/pⁱ⌋ mod p. Combines the vanishing criterion with Lucas's product congruence (choose_modEq_prod_range_choose_nat), transfers divisibility across the congruence, distributes the prime with Prime.dvd_finset_prod_iff, and discharges each factor by the single-digit engine.
sections.mathContext: The exact base-p digit stratification the open question asked for: surviving orders are precisely the digit-dominated k, reaching up to k = m in the unbounded regime m ≥ p.

sections.title: The Digit Count Realized over 𝔽₂
sections.summary: nonzero_orders_X3_F2: over 𝔽₂, hasseDeriv k (X³) ≠ 0 ↔ k ≤ 3 (3 = 11₂ dominates all k ≤ 3; count 2·2 = 4). nonzero_orders_X4_F2: hasseDeriv k (X⁴) ≠ 0 ↔ k ∈ {0,4} (4 = 100₂; count 1·1·2 = 2). hasseDeriv_X4_F2_profile: the explicit profile — orders 1,2,3 vanish, orders 0 and 4 survive. Orders above the degree are killed by hasseDeriv_eq_zero_of_lt_natDegree; the rest by kernel decide.
sections.mathContext: The Glaisher/Fine count ∏(dᵢ + 1) of nonzero binomials realized concretely, showing survival in the m ≥ p regime is a genuine digit phenomenon, dense (X³) or sparse (X⁴).

conclusion.summary: A fully verified (0 sorries, 0 axioms, no native_decide) file of 198 lines and 9 theorems answering the parent's first open question. Over a field of characteristic p, the Hasse derivative hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) is nonzero exactly when the k-th binomial coefficient C(m,k) survives mod p, which by Lucas's theorem happens precisely when every base-p digit of k is dominated by the corresponding digit of m. In the unbounded regime m ≥ p — where the ordinary derivative test is blind — the surviving orders are the digit-dominated k, a sublattice of [0,m] whose size is the Glaisher/Fine product ∏(dᵢ + 1) over the base-p digits of m, realized concretely over 𝔽₂ by X³ (all four orders) and X⁴ (only k ∈ {0,4}).
conclusion.implications: This refines the parent's coarse dichotomy into a sharp per-order description. 'Blind for m ≥ p' is a statement about the ordinary derivatives; the correct Hasse derivatives carry a rich digit-carved survival pattern. The result identifies exactly which higher-order Hasse data is available in positive characteristic — relevant to inseparability detection, Wronskian/gap-sequence analysis of curves in characteristic p, and the combinatorics of Pascal's triangle mod p (Sierpiński-type patterns) that the surviving-order sets reproduce.
openQuestions: Extend the digit-domination criterion from the pure power Xᵐ to a general polynomial f: express the surviving-order set of hasseDeriv k f at a root a in terms of the base-p digit structure of the multiplicities appearing in f, and relate it to the overcounting gap of the parent dichotomy.

Quantify the surviving-order count ∏(dᵢ + 1) as a function of m and p (its average order, its extremes, and the density of m for which the ordinary test recovers a positive fraction of the Hasse orders), connecting to Kummer's carry count and the Stolarsky–Harborth constant for base-p digit sums.
